Turf ribbons between pavers on a Hunters Creek walkway

Turf set between pavers, a stepping-stone path or a driveway accent strip, is quoted per job in Hunters Creek rather than a flat per-square-foot rate, since the paver layout and cut count drive most of the cost. The HCCA's own guidelines define a stepping stone as a landscape feature in its own right and require ARC approval for poured concrete curbing, which makes a paver-and-turf path here a two-part decision: the hardscape layout first, the turf ribbons second.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

The association's own glossary already has a word for this

The HCCA's Architectural Guidelines define a stepping stone as a stone integrated into a landscape plan as a feature in its own right, a small detail that matters because it means the association already treats a stepping-stone path as landscaping subject to plan review rather than as an incidental addition. A turf-and-paver design, stones or pavers set with ribbons of grass or synthetic turf running between them, falls under that same landscape-plan review, and poured concrete curbing anywhere in the layout needs its own separate ARC sign-off with color samples and a border photo submitted alongside the plan.

Why the cut count, not the square footage, sets the price

A straight paver walkway with turf ribbons on either side is a simple layout to price, but a curved stepping-stone path through a planting bed multiplies the cuts a crew has to make, since turf comes in wide rolls that run one direction and every stone edge needs its own trimmed piece. On a typical lot here, where many villages were built with paver driveway extensions and accent walkways as standard builder features, retrofitting turf between existing pavers usually costs more per square foot than the same turf laid as one open panel, purely from the added labor of all those edges.

One grade, two base materials under a Hunters Creek ribbon

Pavers want a dense-graded aggregate compacted tight enough to carry a tire's point load, while the turf beside them needs the opposite: a washed, open-graded crushed rock or crushed concrete layer that lets water pass straight through instead of locking together. On a Hunters Creek paver-and-turf job the two materials meet at a single finished grade set before either one goes down, so the strip doesn't sit proud of or sunk below the hardscape once both are compacted. Keeping the layout continuous while letting the base underneath change at the joint is what makes the two materials behave as one surface instead of two competing ones.

Brushing infill into a narrow strip by hand

Infill on an open lawn gets broadcast and worked in with a drop spreader, but a Hunters Creek ribbon only a few inches wide gets its infill brushed in by hand instead, since a spreader throws material past the strip and into the paver joints on either side. Working infill in against the grain with a stiff brush, a little at a time, keeps the rate close to the standard one to two pounds per square foot without overloading the joint sand next to it. This last step takes longer per square foot than an open lawn does, which is part of why a narrow strip prices differently than its size alone would suggest.

Say you have a 200 sq ft ribbon along a paver walkway

Say you have a 40-foot paver walkway from the driveway to the front entry with an 18-inch turf ribbon planned on each side, roughly 200 sq ft of turf in narrow strips once both sides are added up. Priced at labor rates closer to the $8–$18 range for the turf portion alone, plus the added time for two long, narrow cuts instead of one open panel, a ribbon job like this typically lands above what 200 sq ft of open lawn would cost, which is why it's quoted from the actual layout rather than a flat number.

Matching backing drainage to a strip boxed in by pavers

An open lawn's backing has an entire yard to spread water across if one section runs slow, but a Hunters Creek turf strip pinned between two paver courses doesn't have that margin, so the backing's drainage rating matters more here than the square footage would suggest. A product rated to pass more than thirty inches of water an hour clears a joint fast enough that a hose rinse or a summer downpour doesn't linger against either paver edge. Choosing a lower-rated backing to save cost on a small strip is one of the few places where the square footage saved doesn't offset the drainage lost.

What the base looks like when pavers are already in place

Turf going in between pavers that are already set doesn't get the same clean excavate-and-compact sequence a fresh lawn conversion does, since the crew works around fixed hardscape rather than an open bed. A thinner, well-compacted base gets built in each gap, sized to sit flush with the paver surface once turf and infill are in, and drainage has to move water down through that narrow strip rather than across a broad graded yard, which matters on the area's slow-draining sand even at this smaller scale.

Narrow strips lift first when wind gets under an edge

A wide lawn has enough turf and infill weight spread across its footprint to resist wind getting underneath any one spot, but a narrow ribbon or stepping-stone path on a Hunters Creek property has far less material per linear foot of edge, so a gust that would barely move a full lawn can catch and lift a thin strip's corner. That's part of why edge anchoring gets extra attention on this kind of layout; a nail spacing that's adequate on an open yard can leave a narrow strip more exposed than the same standard would suggest.

Walking the paver edge after a named storm

After heavy wind or rain, the paver-and-turf joint on a Hunters Creek property is worth checking specifically, since the anchor points along that edge carry more stress per linear foot than a full lawn's perimeter does. A nail that's started to pull loose near a paver course, or a corner that's lifted a fraction of an inch, is easier to re-secure the same week than after it's had another storm to work at it. This check takes only a few minutes along a ribbon or path, far less time than the same walk around an open lawn's full perimeter.

Questions people ask

Do I need ARC approval just for turf ribbons between existing pavers?

Likely yes, since the association's guideline treats a landscape change tied to a hardscape feature as part of the same plan review a stepping-stone path or paver walkway already falls under.

Is turf between pavers cheaper than turfing the whole yard?

Not per square foot. Narrow strips with more cuts and edges typically cost more per foot than one open panel of the same total area, even though the total project is smaller.
